---
title: Results
toc: false
---

What each solver in Mosaic can do on each benchmark setup: whether its
forward solution, gradient and optimization results are good enough for the
task, what it costs relative to its peers, and how much of the campaign ran
cleanly. Mosaic does not rank solvers or combine these into a single score.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
These are **example results**, produced automatically on GitHub Actions runners
and refreshed on every release. Accuracy and gradient metrics are
hardware-independent and reproducible; wall-clock numbers reflect commodity
cloud hardware and are best read as relative scaling between solvers. For
numbers that reflect *your* setup, [run the benchmarks
yourself](getting-started.qmd) on your target hardware.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Results reflect the current implementations, not the libraries"}
Each solver is wrapped in a Tesseract by the Mosaic team or its contributors.
A flag or a slow time here says how *this implementation* behaves on *this
setup*, not how good the underlying software is. The **Effort** column shows
how far each wrapper had to go beyond documented use, and **Deviations** where
it runs a substitute for part of the setup. Solvers that pass the same checks
can differ a lot in how much work a new setup takes, so try the alternatives
before committing to one.

If you maintain or use one of these solvers and can improve its
configuration, [contributions are welcome](https://github.com/pasteurlabs/mosaic/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).
:::

## How to read the checks {#reading}

Results are grouped by **setup**: one concrete problem statement, such as
periodic Taylor–Green flow or channel flow past a cylinder. Setups of the same
physics are not averaged, because a solver that handles one need not handle
the other.

For each setup, each solver gets:

- **Forward, gradient and optimization checks.** Every experiment carries pass
  criteria set in its problem configuration (`status_check`): for example an
  error bound against the reference, a finite-difference agreement bound for
  the gradient, or the fraction of the objective an optimizer must remove. A
  check combines the setup's *gate* experiments for that suite (see the table
  of states below). Hover a check for each gate's headline numbers and the
  reasons for any flag; the list under each table spells the reasons out.
- **Cost**, forward and VJP: wall-clock time as a multiple of the fastest
  solver *on the same kind of device*, at the largest problem size every
  solver in that group completed. GPU and CPU solvers ran on different
  machines, so they are compared within their group only; a solver sits in
  the group its cost results were measured on, and a note marks results that
  ran on another device than the solver now targets. A **≈** marks a gap
  to the fastest solver that is no larger than twice the spread (standard
  deviation) of the two solvers' timed trials, so the two cannot be told apart
  on this run. Hover a cost for the mean, its spread, the number of trials and
  the first call, which includes compilation and setup. The per-suite tables
  on each results page give the absolute times.
- **Reliability**: how many of the setup's experiments ran cleanly, out of
  those the solver supports, with flagged, failed, blocked and not-run
  experiments counted separately. This includes diagnostic experiments that
  are not gates (Jacobian spectra, horizon sweeps, cost sweeps). A cost run
  flagged only for being slow counts as clean here; its speed shows in the
  cost columns. **Resource limits** counts the sweeps a solver completed only
  up to some size or rollout length before running out of memory or time;
  where those limits lie depends on the hardware.
- **Effort**: the highest level among the interventions a solver *needs* on
  that setup, from L0 (documented options) and L1 (undocumented configuration)
  to L2 (user code on the library's public primitives) and L3 (changes to the
  solver itself). A filter above the tables hides solvers above the level you
  are willing to work at yourself.
- **Deviations**: where a solver runs a substitute for the prescribed setup,
  such as a different outflow condition, with its effect on the results.

The [Solver Reference](solvers.qmd) lists every intervention with its reason,
evidence and upstream issue, including those nobody has a reason for yet.

::: {.ck-legend}
| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| [✓ Pass]{.ck .ck-pass} | Every gate experiment met its criteria. |
| [! Borderline]{.ck .ck-borderline} | A gate was flagged: it ran, but missed its criteria. A superscript *i* means every flag has a documented cause, often a property of the method or of the comparison rather than of the implementation; hover for the explanation. |
| [✗ Fail]{.ck .ck-fail} | A gate errored or produced no valid result. |
| [⊘ Blocked]{.ck .ck-blocked} | The gates are excluded for a recorded reason that may be lifted: the solver is unstable on them, they are infeasible within the time or memory budget, an upstream bug stops them, or the wrapper does not implement them yet. The cell names the reason. |
| [— Not supported]{.ck .ck-na} | The method cannot express the experiment, e.g. a forward-only solver has no gradient. |
| [· Not run]{.ck .ck-notrun} | Not run in this campaign yet. |
:::

Within each device group, solvers that pass more checks are listed first, then
faster ones. That ordering is a reading aid, not a ranking: a solver that
passes everything is not "better" than one that is flagged on a check your
application does not need.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Gate experiments per setup"}
{{< include _gates.qmd >}}

Some criteria are absolute: an error bound against an analytic solution or a
converged reference run, an observed order of convergence, or a minimum
agreement with finite differences. Others compare a solver with the other
solvers on the same experiment, for example an error more than three times
the median of its peers. A flag on a relative criterion says that a solver is
an outlier among its peers, not that it misses an accuracy the task needs. The
thresholds are provisional and will be refined with the solver maintainers;
they live next to each experiment in
`mosaic/benchmarks/problems/<domain>/config.py`.
:::

## Domains

Each domain page collects the setups of one physics problem and reports, per
suite: **forward** (output against a trusted reference, and an analytic
solution where one exists), **gradient** (AD or adjoint gradient against a
finite-difference ground truth, in magnitude and direction), **cost** (forward
and VJP wall-clock scaling with problem size) and **optimization** (end-to-end
convergence using each solver's own gradients). See the
[Overview](index.qmd#evaluation-protocol) for the full evaluation protocol.

[F2]{.domain-id .d-F2}

[[Navier–Stokes (2D)](results_ns_grid.qmd)]{.domain-card-title}

Optimize the inflow of a 2D channel flow to minimize drag on a cylinder,
differentiating through an incompressible fluid solver. Covers JAX-CFD,
PhiFlow, INS.jl, XLB, PICT, Warp-NS, and OpenFOAM across spectral,
finite-difference, finite-volume, and LBM schemes.
:::

[F3]{.domain-id .d-F3}

[[Navier–Stokes (3D)](results_ns_3d_grid.qmd)]{.domain-card-title}

Recover the initial velocity field of a 3D turbulent flow from a later snapshot,
differentiating through the Navier–Stokes rollout. Covers PhiFlow, XLB, PICT,
Warp-NS, Exponax, INS.jl, and OpenFOAM on a triply periodic Taylor–Green vortex.

[[Structural mechanics](results_structural_mesh.qmd)]{.domain-card-title}

Place a fixed budget of material in a clamped beam to make it as stiff as
possible, differentiating through a finite-element solve. Covers deal.II,
FEniCS, Firedrake, JAX-FEM, TopOpt.jl, and torch-fem on 2D cantilever compliance
minimization with SIMP penalization.
